title: Kinds of consciousness
hookLine: the manuals count 89 types of consciousness; the point is to see how varied mind is

cards: At the paint store there's a wall of little color cards, and a whole stretch of it is white. Eggshell. Linen.
Held up one by one, they all look like white. Laid side by side, they're plainly different, warm and cool, bright and dull, and a person who works with paint can tell them apart at a glance.
The mind, from the inside, can seem a bit like plain white: just me, thinking. The Abhidhamma holds up the cards side by side.

teach.b: A manual this path has been leaning on, the Abhidhammattha Sangaha, counts the kinds of consciousness, citta, and its count is eighty-nine. It isn't really meant as a test. It's a way of showing how varied mind is.
First, it sorts by where a moment belongs.

teach.h: SORTED BY WORLD AND BY ROOT.
teach.b: Some belong to ordinary life in the world of the senses: seeing a bus, wanting a sandwich. Some belong to deep meditation, states the texts describe as calm and bright. And some belong to the moments of awakening itself.
Second, it sorts by roots. Some moments are rooted in greed, some in aversion, some in confusion; others in their opposites: generosity, kindness, understanding.
Third, it notices the feeling that comes along: pleasure, a flat, neutral tone, or displeasure. Fourth, a smaller detail.

teach.h: ON ITS OWN, OR AFTER A PUSH.
teach.b: The manual separates moments that arise on their own from moments that needed a push, from yourself or from someone else.

So a kind act done spontaneously and the same act done after a friend nudged you count as two different kinds of mind. Neither is thrown out. The nudged kindness is still kindness, but they're not the same card.
What's the use of all this sorting on an ordinary Tuesday? It loosens a habit. It's easy to say I'm an anxious person, or I'm a generous person, as if the mind were one color.

teach.h: CARD BY CARD, THE MIND IS MANY.
teach.b: Card by card, the mind is many: anxious moments, generous moments, bored moments, tender moments, each arising and passing, and none of them the whole wall.

how: Students of the Abhidhamma in Theravada communities learn the manual's list of the kinds of consciousness, often with charts, and teachers use it to help meditators recognize the many states of mind they meet.

practice: If you'd like, look back over the last day and find three different moments of mind: one bright, a laugh or a good bite of food; one heavy, an annoyance or a worry; one flat, waiting or standing in line.
Hold each up like a color card, side by side, and notice that each one passed. Then rest with whatever kind of mind is here now, and see if you can name its color.

wordCard.voice: Kinds of consciousness. One manual counts eighty-nine, sorted by world, by root and by feeling, to show how varied the mind is. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali: consciousness, the knowing; in the manuals used alongside citta for a moment of mind.
